actionThatDiffers: You jump straight to the one session that matters instead of tab-cycling 8 panes to work out which is which; you also stop re-opening the wrong pane twice a day.
why: Briefing: a session s own state is fully visible in its own terminal, and Claude Code has harness-generated session titles. A tmux list-panes + capture-pane sweep plus cwd from ps yields an adequate approximation of what each session is, so rule 2 caps access at 60; distilling a one-line identity for 8 panes is still manual reading, hence mid-40s rather than 30. Split assumed: Claude Code supplies titles natively, the other nine harnesses supply none, so cross-harness this is scrollback reading. Impact is real but bounded - it changes which pane you visit, not whether work is lost.

actionThatDiffers: A review request the agent raises gets filed as a Spacedock gate the captain later clears in a batch, instead of being answered inline in whichever pane raised it.
why: Not covered by the briefing beyond the mention that Cargento renders Spacedock workflow stage strips, so confidence low. Rule 5: this is something the user or the workflow DOES, so access is how hard it is to do today - a user already running Spacedock types one prompt or runs the workflow command to open a gate, which the 21-40 band covers. Impact is narrow: it only differs for the subset of users running Spacedock workflows at all, and the underlying review still gets answered either way - it just lands in a queue rather than at the pane.

actionThatDiffers: You revert a force-push or restore a deleted file within minutes of it happening, and you add a guardrail to the session that did it, rather than discovering the loss days later when the branch is gone.
why: Briefing: no harness retains queryable history across sessions, and no harness distinguishes a wedged agent from a productive one. Irreversible acts scroll off the pane, so a capture-pane sweep does not recover them - rule 2 does not rescue this. Traces do exist by hand (git reflog, shell history, transcript files on disk) but attributing them to a session across 8 panes and across time is exactly the 61-80 correlating case. dependsOnDetector true: which tool calls count as irreversible is a heuristic classification over transcripts, not a field any harness records. Impact high because the differing action prevents concrete lost work.

actionThatDiffers: You spot that two sessions are converging on the same file or that one has drifted off the goal you gave it, and you kill or redirect one instead of letting both land conflicting work.
why: Each session s goal is individually visible - the opening prompt is in its own scrollback and in its transcript on disk - so the inputs sit in the 0-40 band and the item is an aggregation over them. Rule 3 caps the roll-up at 60, and rule 2 gives a partial approximation from a capture-pane sweep of current activity. It lands mid-50s rather than lower because current activity is not the goal: recovering intent means scrolling up in every pane, which is several places plus manual work. Split assumed: no harness surfaces the originating goal of any session other than the one in front of you, per the briefing s cross-cutting facts, so this is uniform across all ten.

actionThatDiffers: You go to the session that needs you now instead of round-robining every pane, so an agent that finished ten minutes ago does not sit idle until your next sweep.
why: Briefing lists tmux list-panes and list-windows plus ps under what a resourceful user could do unaided, and rule 2 makes the pane loop an adequate approximation of a roster. Enumerating sessions is the cheapest thing on this board: one command, in a place the user already knows to look, since the panes are his own. It is not 0-20 because no harness shows anything about other sessions, so the user must type something. Split assumed: every session lives in a terminal pane on this one machine - detached, hosted or other-machine sessions are a different item and would score far higher. Impact 65: it changes which pane you visit on a regular basis and reclaims idle agent wall-clock, but rule 6 applies - shipped does not earn a premium.

actionThatDiffers: You move a mechanical session - a lint burndown, a doc sweep - off the expensive model onto the cheap one, so the expensive quota window survives the afternoon.
why: Briefing: Claude Code has a configurable status line and Codex a native usage line in its TUI, and the model is standard status-line content, so per session this is already on screen or one command away. The cross-session view is a sweep of those lines - rule 2 gives it directly and rule 3 caps a sort or comparison over 0-40 inputs at 60, so low 30s is right. Split assumed: Claude Code and Codex surface the model natively; the remaining harnesses vary, but the user chose the model at launch, which is why impact is capped. The differing action is real but occasional - most users already know what they started each session on, so the information mostly saves a check rather than changing a decision.

actionThatDiffers: With a quota window closing you stop the one runaway session and let the other seven finish, instead of stopping everything or letting the window blow and losing all of them mid-turn.
why: Briefing: quota is shown as a current figure, no harness projects a burn rate forward or attributes consumption to a particular session. But rule 2 bites here - which pane is scrolling fastest is an adequate approximation of which session is burning fastest, and a developer can eyeball that in one sweep, so this cannot sit in the 61-80 band. Held to 56 because the eyeball ranking ignores model price and input-token cost, and the numeric version needs a script over transcript token counts. dependsOnDetector true: the rate is a heuristic over a recent window and quota attribution per session is exposed by nothing anywhere. Impact 70 - the differing action protects a blown quota window and the in-flight turns of the sessions you did not kill.

actionThatDiffers: You stop re-triaging a session you already dealt with - the third sweep of the day does not re-surface it, so you do not re-open a pane to confirm what you already know.
why: Rule 5: this is something the user DOES, so access is how hard it is to perform. It is one click or one keystroke - squarely the 21-40 band - and today the equivalent act, mentally writing a session off, costs nothing at all. There is no toggle today only because there is no board today, and rule 4 s nonexistent-versus-withheld distinction does not lift an action s access. Impact is a mild convenience by rule 1: nothing is lost by lacking it, but without it a board of ten sessions accumulates handled rows and stops being scannable, which is a recurring low-grade blocker rather than a prevented loss.

actionThatDiffers: You start the next large task on the harness that still has headroom rather than the one whose window is nearly spent, so the task finishes instead of dying mid-turn and being restarted from scratch.
why: Rule 3 does not apply because the inputs are not all individually visible. Split assumed: Claude Code exposes quota via /usage and Barista caches 5-hour and weekly percentages locally, Codex shows a native usage line - those two are 21-40 alone. The other eight harnesses in the briefing have quota display absent on most, so for them no number exists to fetch at any price. A combined comparison therefore means visiting several harnesses and still having holes, which is the 61-80 correlating band. dependsOnDetector true: for the harnesses with no quota surface any capacity figure rests on a heuristic, and no harness anywhere combines across subscriptions. Impact 76 - the differing action prevents a blown quota window and the wasted hours of a restarted long task.
